passage: Guests were coming in ten minutes, and Mummy was still frying pakoras. "Gurleen, can you help?" Gurleen, six, put down her doll. She stacked the scattered cushions, pushed the shoes under the bench and gave her little brother Irfan a job: "You carry the spoons, one by one." Irfan dropped two. Gurleen picked them up, rinsed them at the sink and dried them on the towel. When the doorbell rang, the table had six plates and a spoon beside each. Mummy looked in and blinked. "Who did all this?"

qa.q: How many plates were on the table when the bell rang?
qa.a: Six plates, with a spoon beside each.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen rinse the dropped spoons?
qa.a: She seemed determined to do the job properly and wanted things clean for the guests.

qa.q: How could Mummy show she noticed Gurleen's help?
qa.a: She could thank her by name and give her a regular small job, so she keeps feeling useful at home.

qa.q: What is it like for Irfan to be given the spoon job?
qa.a: He gets to feel part of the work even though he drops a few, and he learns from his sister.

grounding: It shows a young child helping with age-appropriate chores and keeping things clean under time pressure.

passage: At the end of art time in their Delhi school, the shared crayon box lay open on the floor, with three crayons rolling under the table. Tarun, five, crawled under and collected them. Simran was peeling the paper off a blue crayon in long strips. "Don't," Tarun said. "Ma'am said the class crayons are for everyone. If you peel them, they break." Simran stopped and dropped the strips in the dustbin. Tarun lined the crayons up by colour, closed the lid and put the box back on the shelf.

qa.q: How many crayons were rolling under the table?
qa.a: Three crayons were rolling under the table.

qa.q: Why did Tarun tell Simran to stop peeling?
qa.a: He cared about the shared crayons lasting and remembered Ma'am saying they are for everyone.

qa.q: How could the teacher support children like Tarun?
qa.a: She could give a "crayon keeper" role each week, so caring for class things becomes everyone's job in turn.

qa.q: How might Simran feel when Tarun stops her?
qa.a: She might feel a bit embarrassed or annoyed, but she stops and bins the strips, suggesting she accepts it.

grounding: It shows a young child respecting and looking after shared classroom property and keeping the space clean.

passage:
"Abbu, the plants look thirsty."
"You're right, Ojas. Want to water them?"
"Can I use the big can?"
"Too heavy. Use the small mug and fill it many times."
Ojas trudged back and forth from the bathroom. "One pot... two pots..."
"Careful, the floor's getting wet."
"Oops." Ojas fetched the old cloth and wiped the tiles, tongue poking out.
"Look at that. Clean floor and happy plants."
"Tomorrow can I do it again? It's my job now."
Wasim laughed. "Your job now."

qa.q: What did Ojas use to water the plants?
qa.a: The small mug, filled many times.

qa.q: What does "It's my job now" suggest about how Ojas feels?
qa.a: He feels proud and grown-up having a real household task, and he wants to keep it. 😊

qa.q: Which of Wasim's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Giving a small mug instead of the heavy can made the chore possible for a young child, and pointing out the wet floor let Ojas fix it himself.

qa.q: What would change if Wasim had wiped the floor himself?
qa.a: Ojas would miss learning to clean up after his own work and might not feel the whole job was his.

grounding: It shows a young child taking on a home chore and cleaning up after himself.

passage:

Today after painting, Siddharth took the dirty water cups to the sink without being asked and wiped the table with a cloth. He put the class scissors back in their box, counting them. qa.q: How might Siddharth's parents respond to this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel proud and might give him small jobs at home as well.

grounding: Illustrates a young child helping with chores, caring for shared classroom property and keeping surroundings clean.

passage: At dawn in their village, Kavitha swept the courtyard with a long broom. Keerthana, six, carried the small brass pot to fill the tulsi plant. She put her slippers neatly by the door. Before school she wiped her slate, which she shared with her cousin, and wrapped the chalk in a cloth. 'Amma, I put the broom back too,' she called. Kavitha smiled and handed her a piece of jaggery.

qa.q: What did Keerthana carry to the tulsi plant?
qa.a: She carried the small brass pot to fill it.

qa.q: What might Keerthana be feeling when she calls out about the broom?
qa.a: She probably feels proud of helping and wants Amma to notice.

qa.q: How could Kavitha keep Keerthana's help going as she grows?
qa.a: She could give her slightly bigger jobs over time and thank her, so helping becomes part of her day.

qa.q: How might Keerthana's cousin see her care with the shared slate?
qa.a: The cousin would likely appreciate finding the slate clean and the chalk safe.

grounding: Shows a young child doing small household chores and caring for shared property in a village home.

passage: In their Singapore flat, Xin, five, pulled a chair up to the counter. "Can I help?" Her father Javier handed her the spoons. She set them next to each plate, then went back for the cups. After dinner she took her own plate to the sink and dropped her orange peel in the bin, not on the table. Javier noticed and said, "Thank you, chef." Xin grinned and asked if she could wipe the table too.

qa.q: What did Javier hand Xin?
qa.a: The spoons.

qa.q: How might Xin feel when Javier calls her "chef"?
qa.a: She feels proud and happy that her help was noticed.

qa.q: How could Javier build on Xin's helping?
qa.a: Give her a small regular job, like setting the spoons, so she feels part of the family routine.

qa.q: What would change if Javier had said "Go and play, I'll do it"?
qa.a: Xin might stop offering to help and miss out on learning the routine.

grounding: Shows a young child helping set the table and cleaning up after herself at home.

passage: At kindergarten, it was tidy-up time. Charu, five, noticed the glue stick without its cap on the art table. She found the cap under a chair, clicked it on, and put it in the box. Then she saw paint spilled on the floor. "Ma'am, spill!" she called. Disha, the teacher, gave her a cloth. Charu wiped slowly and carefully, then held up the cloth. "All clean!"

qa.q: Where did Charu find the glue stick's cap?
qa.a: Under a chair.

qa.q: What does Charu holding up the cloth and saying "All clean!" suggest?
qa.a: She felt proud of taking care of the classroom.

qa.q: How could Disha support Charu's care for class things?
qa.a: Thank her and give everyone small tidy-up jobs so looking after shared things becomes normal.

qa.q: How might the other children be affected by Charu's tidying?
qa.a: They find the glue working and the floor safe to walk on.

grounding: Shows a young child taking care of shared classroom things and cleaning up a spill.

passage: I'm Raghav, from the house next door. Every morning Binita's mother sweeps their courtyard. This week Binita, who's five, got her own small broom. She sweeps the leaves into a pile by the gate, very seriously, and picks up the sweet wrappers the wind blows in. Yesterday she carried the pile to the compost pit in her skirt. I can't say why she enjoys it, but she looked proud when her mother clapped.

qa.q: What did Binita get this week?
qa.a: Her own small broom.

qa.q: What might Binita have felt when her mother clapped?
qa.a: She seemed proud and pleased that her work was noticed.

qa.q: How could Binita's mother support this habit?
qa.a: Keep sweeping together and praise her effort, so helping feels like part of family life.

qa.q: How does Raghav see Binita's sweeping?
qa.a: Raghav notices how seriously she does it, but only guesses at why she enjoys it.

grounding: Shows a young child helping keep the courtyard clean, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Monday: At the end of play, Arohi left crayons all over the floor of the classroom. Sarita Ma'am picked them up while Arohi ran to the door.
Wednesday: Sarita Ma'am gave her a small basket. "This is the crayon home. Can you help me?" Arohi dropped them in one by one, humming.
The next Monday: Before anyone asked, Arohi put the caps back on the markers, filled the basket and watered the class plant. "I'm the helper!" she told her mother at pickup.

qa.q: What did Sarita Ma'am give Arohi on Wednesday?
qa.a: A small basket for the crayons.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel when she told her mother, "I'm the helper!"?
qa.a: She felt proud and pleased with her new job.

qa.q: How might Arohi's mother feel hearing "I'm the helper!"?
qa.a: She would likely feel happy and proud that her daughter is taking responsibility at school.

grounding: Across a week, a young girl goes from leaving crayons out to tidying and watering the class plant on her own.

passage: The monsoon had knocked out the power in Guwahati, and everything smelled damp. Hemant lit a candle and began folding the washing he'd dried indoors. Binita, five, came to help. "Socks are my job," she said. She paired them by feel in the dim light, lining up the small ones. Then she saw the muddy shoes by the door. She carried them to the mat outside and set them in a row. "No mud inside, Papa." Hemant laughed. "Our house boss."

qa.q: What was Hemant doing by candlelight?
qa.a: Folding the washing he'd dried indoors.

qa.q: What does Binita saying "Socks are my job" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud and responsible, happy to have her own part in the chores.

qa.q: How could Hemant keep encouraging Binita's help?
qa.a: He could keep giving her small jobs like the socks and thank her for noticing the muddy shoes.

qa.q: How might the dark, damp evening feel different for Hemant because of Binita's help?
qa.a: The chores would feel lighter and more fun, and he enjoys his daughter's care for the house. 😊

grounding: During a monsoon power cut, a small girl pairs socks and moves muddy shoes out to keep the house clean.

passage: A week before Diwali, the whole flat in Chembur smelled of wet cloth. Kamal Chacha was scrubbing the high shelves. Jeevan, five, got a damp rag of his own. "I'll do the low ones," he said. He wiped each shelf slowly, putting the small brass lamps back exactly where they were. Then he swept the dust from under the sofa into a pile. "Look, Chacha!" Kamal Chacha peered down. "Very neat. Now carry it to the bin with me."

qa.q: What was Kamal Chacha scrubbing?
qa.a: The high shelves.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he called, "Look, Chacha!"?
qa.a: He felt proud of his work and eager to show it.

qa.q: What did Kamal Chacha do that made Jeevan's help work?
qa.a: He let Jeevan take the low shelves and praised the neat job, then did the last step together.

qa.q: How might the Diwali cleaning feel for Kamal Chacha with Jeevan helping?
qa.a: It would feel less of a chore and more of a shared job with his young nephew.

grounding: A five-year-old helps with Diwali cleaning by wiping low shelves and sweeping dust.

passage:
"Can I help, Mumma?" Hansa asked. It was Diwali cleaning day.

"Yes. Wipe the diyas with this cloth," Sonali said.

Hansa wiped each one and lined them up. "Done! What next?"

"Put your toys in the basket."

Hansa carried every toy, even the ones under the bed. "Now my room is clean for Lakshmi!"

Sonali laughed. "You're a big help."

qa.q: How did Hansa feel while helping?
qa.a: Hansa felt eager and proud to help, asking what to do next.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel with Hansa's help?

passage:

passage:
After the harvest festival in the village near Hisar, the courtyard was full of leaves and paper. Yash and Noor, both five, got small brooms.

"You sweep, I'll pick up the paper," Yash said.

Noor swept the leaves into a pile. Yash put the paper in the bin. Then he watered Dadi's tulsi plant.

Dadi came out. "Who cleaned my courtyard?"

"We did!"

qa.q: What did Yash water?
qa.a: He watered Dadi's tulsi plant.

qa.q: How did Yash and Noor feel when Dadi asked who cleaned?
qa.a: They felt proud and happy, shouting "We did!"

qa.q: How can Dadi encourage their helping?
qa.a: She can thank them and give them small jobs like sweeping and watering regularly.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel seeing the clean courtyard?
qa.a: Dadi was likely pleased and surprised.

grounding: After a harvest festival, two young children help sweep the courtyard and care for the plants.

passage: The week before Eid in Amman, everyone in Siddiq's flat was cleaning. Siddiq's job was to match the shoes by the door and wipe the low windowsill. He did it slowly, tongue between his teeth. His sister Nour swept, and when he tipped the dustpan too early she groaned, "Siddiq!" He scooped the dust back up himself. At school the next day, he noticed the class glue sticks lying uncapped. He capped each one and put them back in the tray before anyone asked.

qa.q: What was Siddiq's job at home?
qa.a: To match the shoes by the door and wipe the low windowsill.

qa.q: How did Siddiq feel when Nour groaned at him?
qa.a: He probably felt a little embarrassed but responsible, so he scooped the dust back up himself.

qa.q: How could Siddiq's teacher encourage his care for class things?
qa.a: The teacher could thank him quietly and give him a small class job, like checking the glue tray each day.

qa.q: How does Nour see Siddiq's help?
qa.a: Nour is irritated by the spilled dust at first, but may appreciate that Siddiq fixes his own mistake.

grounding: Shows a young child doing small chores before a festival and looking after shared classroom things.
